packs.title: Quadratics and discriminants
packs.instructions: Answer on separate paper. Show your working. Give exact answers unless a decimal is requested.

questions.question: Solve $x^2-5x+6=0$ by factorisation.
questions.questionText: Solve $x^2-5x+6=0$ by factorisation.
steps: 1. Find two numbers with product 6 and sum -5: -2 and -3.
3. Set each factor equal to zero: $x=2$ or $x=3$.

questions.question: Solve $2x^2+3x-7=0$. Give exact answers.
questions.questionText: Solve $2x^2+3x-7=0$. Give exact answers.

3. Apply the quadratic formula: $x=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{65}}{2(2)}$.
4. Simplify the denominator to 4; retain the surd for exact answers.

questions.question: Write $2x^2-8x+3$ in completed-square form. Hence state the vertex and minimum value.
questions.questionText: Write $2x^2-8x+3$ in completed-square form. Hence state the vertex and minimum value.
steps: 1. Factor the first two terms: $2(x^2-4x)+3$.
2. Complete the square: $x^2-4x=(x-2)^2-4$.
4. The squared term is nonnegative, with value 0 at $x=2$. Hence the minimum is -5 and the vertex is $(2,-5)$.
criteria: M1: Valid completion of the square [1].

questions.question: Find all values of $k$ for which $x^2+(k-2)x+k=0$ has a repeated real root.
questions.questionText: Find all values of $k$ for which $x^2+(k-2)x+k=0$ has a repeated real root.
steps: 1. A repeated root requires discriminant zero.
3. Complete the square: $(k-4)^2=12$.
4. Taking both square roots gives $k=4\pm2\sqrt3$.
criteria: M1: Correct quadratic equation in k [1].

questions.question: Find the range of $c$ for which $x^2-6x+c>0$ for every real $x$. Explain why the boundary is excluded.
questions.questionText: Find the range of $c$ for which $x^2-6x+c>0$ for every real $x$. Explain why the boundary is excluded.
steps: 1. Complete the square: $x^2-6x+c=(x-3)^2+c-9$.
2. Its minimum occurs at $x=3$ and equals $c-9$.
3. Strict positivity requires $c-9>0$, so $c>9$.
4. At $c=9$ the expression is zero at $x=3$, so that boundary is excluded.
criteria: M1: Uses the minimum or discriminant correctly [1].
B1: Explains exclusion of the boundary [1].

questions.question: The line $y=2x+k$ is tangent to $y=x^2-4x+5$. Find $k$ and the point of contact.
questions.questionText: The line $y=2x+k$ is tangent to $y=x^2-4x+5$. Find $k$ and the point of contact.
steps: 1. At an intersection, $x^2-4x+5=2x+k$, so $x^2-6x+5-k=0$.
2. Tangency requires one repeated intersection: $36-4(5-k)=0$.
4. The equation becomes $(x-3)^2=0$, so $x=3$. Substitute into the line: $y=6-4=2$.

questions.questionText: Solve $e^{2x}-5e^x+4=0$, giving exact values of $x$.

A1: Both exact x values with domain respected [1].

questions.question: A ball has height $h(t)=-5t^2+20t+1$ metres, $t$ seconds after launch. Find its greatest height and when it occurs. Find when it first reaches the ground ($t>0$).
questions.questionText: A ball has height $h(t)=-5t^2+20t+1$ metres, $t$ seconds after launch. Find its greatest height and when it occurs. Find when it first reaches the ground ($t>0$).
questions.answer: Greatest height 21 m at 2 s; ground at $t=2+\dfrac{\sqrt{105}}5\approx4.05$ s.
steps: 1. Complete the square: $h(t)=-5(t-2)^2+21$.
2. The greatest height is 21 m, attained at $t=2$ s because the square has a negative coefficient.
4. Thus $t=2\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{105}}5$. The negative branch is less than zero, so the relevant time is approximately 4.05 s.
criteria: A1: Height and time with units [1].
M1: Correct ground-level equation and roots [1].
A1: Selects the positive time with units [1].

packs.title: Binomial hypothesis testing
packs.instructions: Calculator required. Show hypotheses, probabilities and conclusions. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places.

questions.question: A factory claims a 10% defect rate. A random sample of 20 items contains 5 defects. Test at the 5% level whether the defect rate has increased. Assume independence.
questions.questionText: A factory claims a 10% defect rate. A random sample of 20 items contains 5 defects. Test at the 5% level whether the defect rate has increased. Assume independence.
questions.answer: $p\text{-value}=0.0432$. Reject the claim of p = 0.10; there is evidence that the defect rate has increased.
steps: 1. Let X count defects. Under $H_0:p=0.10$, $X\sim B(20,0.10)$; the alternative is $H_1:p>0.10$.
2. For an upper-tail test, use $P(X\ge5)=1-P(X\le4)=0.0432$.
4. There is sufficient evidence, at the 5% level, that the population defect rate is greater than 10%.
criteria: B1: Correct variable, null model and hypotheses [1].
M1: Uses the correct upper tail [1].

questions.question: A die is rolled independently 60 times and shows six on 4 occasions. Test at the 5% level whether the probability of a six is below $\tfrac16$.
questions.questionText: A die is rolled independently 60 times and shows six on 4 occasions. Test at the 5% level whether the probability of a six is below $\tfrac16$.
questions.answer: $p\text{-value}=0.0202$. Reject $H_0$; evidence that the probability of a six is below $\tfrac16$.
steps: 1. Let X count sixes. Use $H_0:p=\tfrac16$ and $H_1:p<\tfrac16$. Under the null, $X\sim B(60,\tfrac16)$.
2. The observed count is unusually small, so calculate $P(X\le4)=0.0202$.
3. This is below 0.05, so reject $H_0$.
4. There is sufficient evidence that this die gives a six less often than a fair die would.
criteria: B1: Correct null binomial model and hypotheses [1].

questions.question: A coin gives 16 heads in 20 independent tosses. Test at the 5% level whether it is biased. Use an equal-tail two-sided test.
questions.questionText: A coin gives 16 heads in 20 independent tosses. Test at the 5% level whether it is biased. Use an equal-tail two-sided test.
questions.answer: Two-sided $p\text{-value}=0.0118$. Reject fairness; evidence of bias.
steps: 1. Let X count heads. Use $H_0:p=0.5$, $H_1:p\ne0.5$ and $X\sim B(20,0.5)$ under the null.
2. The upper-tail probability is $P(X\ge16)=0.0059$. Compare it with 0.025.
3. Equivalently, double that tail: the two-sided p-value is 0.0118, below 0.05. Reject $H_0$.
4. There is sufficient evidence that the coin is biased; the observation is in the direction of more heads.
criteria: M1: Correct tail and two-sided adjustment [1].

questions.question: Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(12,0.25)$. An upper-tail test has nominal significance 5%. Find its critical region and actual significance level.
questions.questionText: Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(12,0.25)$. An upper-tail test has nominal significance 5%. Find its critical region and actual significance level.
steps: 1. Choose the smallest integer r for which $P(X\ge r)\le0.05$.
3. Therefore the critical region is $X\ge7$ (with $X\le12$).
4. Its actual significance is the null probability of that region, 0.0143, or approximately 1.43%.
criteria: A1: Probabilities on both sides of the cutoff [1].
B1: Actual significance from region probability [1].

questions.question: Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(10,0.5)$. Construct a two-tailed 5% critical region with at most 2.5% in each tail. Find its actual significance.
questions.questionText: Under $H_0$, $X\sim B(10,0.5)$. Construct a two-tailed 5% critical region with at most 2.5% in each tail. Find its actual significance.
steps: 1. The lower-tail target is 0.025. $P(X\le1)=0.0107$, but $P(X\le2)=0.0547>0.025$.
2. Symmetry about 5 gives the upper region $X\ge9$.
3. The full critical region is $X\le1$ or $X\ge9$.
4. Add the two tail probabilities: actual significance is 0.0215 ≈ 2.15%.
criteria: A1: Correct lower cutoff with boundary check [1].
A1: Correct upper cutoff and combined region [1].

questions.question: For $H_0:p=0.40$ against $H_1:p>0.40$, an exact binomial test gives p-value 0.073. State the 5% decision and interpret it without claiming the null is proved.
questions.questionText: For $H_0:p=0.40$ against $H_1:p>0.40$, an exact binomial test gives p-value 0.073. State the 5% decision and interpret it without claiming the null is proved.
questions.answer: Do not reject $H_0$; insufficient evidence that p exceeds 0.40.
steps: 1. Compare the p-value with the significance level: 0.073 > 0.05.
2. Do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence of a population proportion above 0.40.
3. This does not prove p = 0.40; the sample has not supplied strong enough evidence against it.
criteria: A1: Correct decision and contextual direction [1].
B1: Does not equate non-rejection with proof [1].

questions.question: For $H_0:p=0.20$ against $H_1:p>0.20$, $n=20$ and the observed count is 8. A pupil uses $P(X=8)$ as the p-value. Correct the probability and explain.
questions.questionText: For $H_0:p=0.20$ against $H_1:p>0.20$, $n=20$ and the observed count is 8. A pupil uses $P(X=8)$ as the p-value. Correct the probability and explain.
steps: 1. Under the null, $X\sim B(20,0.20)$. The alternative looks for an unusually high count.
2. Include the observed count and every outcome more extreme in that direction: $P(X\ge8)=1-P(X\le7)=0.0321$.
3. A single-outcome probability omits 9, 10, …, 20 and is not the required tail probability.
criteria: B1: Correct null model and tail direction [1].
B1: Explains inclusion of more extreme outcomes [1].

questions.question: A player attempts 20 free throws. Their success probability rises as they warm up. Explain why one binomial model may be unsuitable. State another condition it would require.
questions.questionText: A player attempts 20 free throws. Their success probability rises as they warm up. Explain why one binomial model may be unsuitable. State another condition it would require.
questions.answer: The success probability is not constant; the binomial model also requires independent trials.
steps: 1. A binomial count assumes a fixed number of trials, each with two outcomes and the same success probability.
2. Warming up changes that probability across the attempts, violating the constant-p assumption.
3. The outcomes must also be independent; this would need justification rather than being inferred from a fixed trial count.
criteria: B1: Links its failure to the context [1].
B1: States independence as an additional requirement [1].

packs.title: Resolving forces
packs.instructions: Use g = 9.8 m s⁻². Answer on separate paper. Show force equations; give decimal answers to 3 significant figures.

questions.question: A force is $(6\mathbf i+8\mathbf j)$ N. Find its magnitude and direction, measured above the positive horizontal axis.
questions.questionText: A force is $(6\mathbf i+8\mathbf j)$ N. Find its magnitude and direction, measured above the positive horizontal axis.
questions.answer: 10 N at 53.1° above the positive horizontal.
steps: 1. The perpendicular components are 6 N horizontally and 8 N vertically.
3. Both components are positive. The angle is $\theta=\tan^{-1}(\tfrac86)=53.130\ldots^\circ$.
criteria: M1: Uses the perpendicular components for magnitude [1].

questions.question: Resolve a 20 N force at 30° above the horizontal into horizontal and vertical components.<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 270 110" aria-label="20 newton force at 30 degrees above horizontal"><path d="M50 85H245 M65 92V15" fill="none" stroke="#a9b9b3"/><line x1="65" y1="85" x2="203.56" y2="5" stroke="#146d65" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="203.56,5 195.8978314304372,5.728816034129128 199.09790183276047,11.27133797095306" fill="#146d65"/><text x="210" y="17" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">20 N</text><text x="95" y="76" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">30°</text><text x="249" y="90" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">x</text></svg>
questions.questionText: Resolve a 20 N force at 30° above the horizontal into horizontal and vertical components.     20 N  30°  x
steps: 1. The horizontal component is adjacent to the angle: $20\cos30^\circ=10\sqrt3$ N.
2. The vertical component is opposite: $20\sin30^\circ=10$ N. Both signs are positive.
criteria: A1: Both components with directions and units [1].

questions.question: A particle is in equilibrium under three forces. Two are 12 N right and 5 N up. Find the third force as a vector and give its magnitude.<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 270 105" aria-label="Two perpendicular forces on a particle"><line x1="90" y1="80" x2="235" y2="80" stroke="#146d65" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="235,80 228.0,76.8 228.0,83.2" fill="#146d65"/><line x1="90" y1="80" x2="90" y2="15" stroke="#146d65" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="90,15 86.8,22.0 93.2,22.0" fill="#146d65"/><text x="155" y="68" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">12 N</text><text x="42" y="25" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">5 N</text><circle cx="90" cy="80" r="4" fill="#203b43"/></svg>
questions.questionText: A particle is in equilibrium under three forces. Two are 12 N right and 5 N up. Find the third force as a vector and give its magnitude.      12 N  5 N
steps: 1. The two known forces sum to $(12\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)$ N.
2. Equilibrium means zero resultant, so the third force is their negative, $(-12\mathbf i-5\mathbf j)$ N.
3. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=13$ N.

questions.question: A 4 kg particle slides down a smooth plane inclined at 30°. Find its acceleration down the plane and the normal reaction.<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 270 115" aria-label="Four kilogram block on a smooth 30 degree incline"><path d="M50 100H240 M70 100L230 7L230 100" fill="none" stroke="#657c75" stroke-width="1.6"/><polygon points="137.9,61 162.1,47 152.1,29.7 127.9,43.7" fill="#e9f3ee" stroke="#146d65" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="173" y="38" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">4 kg</text><text x="94" y="96" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">30°</text></svg>
questions.questionText: A 4 kg particle slides down a smooth plane inclined at 30°. Find its acceleration down the plane and the normal reaction.    4 kg  30°
questions.answer: Acceleration 4.90 m s⁻² down the plane; $R=19.6\sqrt3\approx33.9$ N.
steps: 1. Take down the slope as positive. Weight is $mg=4(9.8)=39.2$ N; smooth means no friction.
2. Parallel to the plane: $39.2\sin30^\circ=4a$, giving $a=4.9$ m s⁻².
3. Perpendicular to the plane there is no acceleration: $R=39.2\cos30^\circ=19.6\sqrt3$ N.
criteria: B1: Correct weight components and smooth-plane assumption [1].

questions.question: A 5 kg particle on a smooth horizontal surface is pulled by 20 N at 30° above the horizontal. Find its acceleration and normal reaction.<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 270 105" aria-label="Five kilogram block pulled 30 degrees above horizontal"><path d="M20 93H250" fill="none" stroke="#657c75"/><rect x="55" y="66" width="30" height="27" fill="#e9f3ee" stroke="#146d65"/><line x1="70" y1="80" x2="174" y2="20" stroke="#146d65" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="174,20 166.33758904649315,20.72626329907152 169.53581274882643,26.26985104978256" fill="#146d65"/><text x="185" y="23" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">20 N</text><text x="100" y="79" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">30°</text><text x="210" y="85" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">5 kg</text></svg>
questions.questionText: A 5 kg particle on a smooth horizontal surface is pulled by 20 N at 30° above the horizontal. Find its acceleration and normal reaction.      20 N  30°  5 kg
steps: 1. Horizontally, the driving component is $20\cos30^\circ=10\sqrt3$ N.
2. Apply $F=ma$: $10\sqrt3=5a$, so $a=2\sqrt3$ m s⁻².
3. Vertically there is no acceleration: $R+20\sin30^\circ=5(9.8)$. Hence $R=49-10=39$ N.
criteria: M1: Resolves the applied force correctly [1].
A1: Correct vertical balance and reaction [1].

questions.question: Forces $(6\mathbf i-2\mathbf j)$ N and $(-2\mathbf i+8\mathbf j)$ N act on a 2 kg particle. Find its acceleration vector and acceleration magnitude.
questions.questionText: Forces $(6\mathbf i-2\mathbf j)$ N and $(-2\mathbf i+8\mathbf j)$ N act on a 2 kg particle. Find its acceleration vector and acceleration magnitude.
questions.answer: $(2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)$ m s⁻²; magnitude $\sqrt{13}\approx3.61$ m s⁻².
steps: 1. Add the forces: $\mathbf F=(4\mathbf i+6\mathbf j)$ N.
2. Use the vector equation $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$: $\mathbf a=\tfrac12(4\mathbf i+6\mathbf j)=(2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)$ m s⁻².
3. Magnitude $|\mathbf a|=\sqrt{2^2+3^2}=\sqrt{13}$ m s⁻².
criteria: A1: Correct acceleration magnitude with units [1].

questions.question: A 3 kg particle moves right on a horizontal surface. A 20 N force acts 30° below the horizontal; a resistance of 8 N acts left. Find acceleration and normal reaction.<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 270 115" aria-label="20 newton force at 30 degrees below horizontal"><path d="M25 20H250" fill="none" stroke="#a9b9b3"/><line x1="70" y1="20" x2="174" y2="80" stroke="#146d65" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="174,80 169.53581274882643,73.73014895021743 166.33758904649315,79.27373670092848" fill="#146d65"/><text x="185" y="65" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">20 N</text><text x="104" y="35" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">30°</text><text x="18" y="104" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">force is below horizontal</text></svg>
questions.questionText: A 3 kg particle moves right on a horizontal surface. A 20 N force acts 30° below the horizontal; a resistance of 8 N acts left. Find acceleration and normal reaction.     20 N  30°  force is below horizontal
steps: 1. Resolve the applied force: $20\cos30^\circ=10\sqrt3$ N right and $20\sin30^\circ=10$ N down.
2. Horizontally, $10\sqrt3-8=3a$, so $a=\dfrac{10\sqrt3-8}3$ m s⁻².
3. Vertically, $R=3(9.8)+10=39.4$ N. The downward pull increases the reaction.
criteria: M1: Correct downward and horizontal components [1].
A1: Correct acceleration with resistance subtracted [1].

questions.question: Two light cables support a 100 N load in equilibrium. The left cable makes 30° with the horizontal and the right makes 60°. Find both tensions.<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 270 130" aria-label="Two cables supporting a 100 newton load"><path d="M45 80H225" fill="none" stroke="#a9b9b3" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/><line x1="135" y1="80" x2="67.45" y2="41" stroke="#146d65" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="67.45,41 71.91217857039405,47.271280762804054 75.11217791293205,41.728717798997835" fill="#146d65"/><line x1="135" y1="80" x2="174" y2="12" stroke="#146d65" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="174,12 167.7415526898495,16.480160406287922 173.29327765800585,19.664237961554058" fill="#146d65"/><line x1="135" y1="80" x2="135" y2="116" stroke="#9a6a29" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="135,116 138.2,109.0 131.8,109.0" fill="#9a6a29"/><text x="25" y="33" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">left cable</text><text x="186" y="20" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">right cable</text><text x="86" y="70" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">30°</text><text x="169" y="69" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">60°</text><text x="148" y="116" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#203b43">100 N</text></svg>
questions.questionText: Two light cables support a 100 N load in equilibrium. The left cable makes 30° with the horizontal and the right makes 60°. Find both tensions.         left cable  right cable  30°  60°  100 N
questions.answer: Left tension 50 N; right tension $50\sqrt3\approx86.6$ N.
steps: 1. Let the tensions be L and R. Horizontally, $L\cos30^\circ=R\cos60^\circ$, so $R=\sqrt3L$.
2. Vertically, $L\sin30^\circ+R\sin60^\circ=100$.
3. Substitute: $\tfrac12L+(\sqrt3L)(\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)=100$, so $2L=100$ and $L=50$ N.
4. Then $R=50\sqrt3$ N. Substitution in both balance equations checks equilibrium.
